catalog_quote: Stress is phonemic in Nuaulu but it carries a light functional load. Primary stress generally occurs on the penultimate syllable of a bisyllabic word-root and does not shift with the addition or deletion of affixes. Thus, if a single-syllable suffix is added to the root of such a word, stress would be on the ante-penultimate syllable. ['rana] /rana/ 'grate/parut' [ka-'rana-te] /ka-rana-te/ 'grater/parutan' ... new_statements.relation_note: This is the very passage the catalog's full record for sout2895 ( : classification set by morphology, root-penult stress invariant under affixation, secondary stress on the first syllable of 4+-syllable roots, listed-set exceptions) is built from; the summary row in the target ('rule': '') is just the empty the rule as stated of that record. The quote was re-verified against the page scan p. It refines the WALS coding (14A Penultimate, 15A Fixed), which is correct for bare roots but drops the root-domain (affix-invariant) condition.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root and stays there when prefixes or suffixes are added or removed (e.g. ['rana] 'grate' > [ka-'rana-te] 'grater'; ['raka] 'ocean' > ['raka-ne] 'outsider'; ['sani-ku] 'my shoulder'), so a root plus one suffix syllable carries word-antepenultimate stress and a prefixed monosyllabic root carries final stress. Stress is called phonemic but with a light functional load; syllable weight plays no role in the statement. For bare disyllabic roots the rule reduces to plain penultimate stress (the WALS coding).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Roots of four or more syllables take secondary stress on the first syllable of the root, with primary stress on the root penult: ["saka'hatɛ-nɛ] 'ghost', ["kupa'naha-ne] 'clove', ["kara'tupa] 'chili'. Nothing is said about secondary stress in shorter roots or on affix strings.
new_statements.exceptions: Three classes of 'discrepancies' (pp. 102-103): (1) monosyllabic roots such as /sa/ 'climb', which have no penult; (2) surface stress contrasts created by affixation, e.g. ['osa] 'one' vs [o-'sa] 'they climb', ['apa-na] 'saliva' vs [a-'pana] 'you feed', ['ai-a] 'you eat' vs [a'ia] 'king'; (3) an unexplained residue, some perhaps loans from Indonesian or neighbouring languages, with final or antepenultimate stress: ['aikune] 'beginning', [apa'lam] 'k.o. mango', [asu'wan] 'cassowary', [kari'sa] 'party', [kasi'pi] 'cassava', [sapa'u] 'ring', [sa'wan] 'sunny and drizzling', ['ukura] 'wrapped sago'; further definite loans are said to exist but are not listed. Because these are infrequent, stress is not written in the Nuaulu orthography.
new_statements.identity_note: Bolton's data are South Nuaulu [nxl] per the SIL archive record for the 1990 thesis (Glottolog lists iso_code 'nni; nxl' for the same reference); WALS code 'nua' maps to Glottolog sout2895 and gives both 'Nuaulu, North' and 'Nuaulu, South' as alternative names. Neither the 1989 paper's stress section nor the WALS page names a village or dialect beyond 'Nuaulu'.

tone_statements.quote: The Nuaulu language belongs to the Central-Malayo-Polynesian subgroup of Austronesian languages. It is not tonal. Although Nuaulu language vitality is much more robust than other language groups in central Maluku, particularly among adherents to the traditional religion, even language use among them is beginning to decline.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation, the the domain quotation and the exception quote are all verbatim on printed pp.102-103 (pp.111-112) of the held WILC vol.7 scan, exactly as the locator says; I read the rendered page scan, not just the scanned. (2) The classification rests on a primary, fieldwork-based phonology article (Bolton 1989, SIL/Pattimura WILC 7) with an explicit stress section whose wording directly supports 'morphological' (root-penult, stress does not shift under prefixation or suffixation, surface antepenult with monosyllabic suffixes, contrastive pairs from affixation, secondary stress root-initial in 4+ syllable roots, listed lexical exceptions). Glottolog's descriptive bibliography has only two items, both by Bolton; the unheld one is her 1990 M.A. thesis, not available online per the SIL archive record downloaded now. sources.note: Explicit first-hand statement by the SIL linguist who wrote the only phonology and grammar of Nuaulu (Bolton 1989, 1990) that the language is not tonal (p. 4). The rest of the thesis uses 'tonal inventory/tonal center' only in the musicological sense (song scales); text-setting discussion notes melodies adjusted to syllable count and metered recitation 'with emphasis on every third or fourth syllable determined by word stress' (p. 38), i.e. prosody is stress-based.
